W7172336769.a1.text: Critics claim simplicity reduces God to an abstract property and makes theological language vacuous.
W7172336769.a1.quote: Critics of divine simplicity argue that simplicity leads us to identify God with an abstract property and that it renders theological language semantically vacuous because divine simplicity cannot ground a plurality of true intrinsic predicates.

W7172336769.a2.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy keeps theological language determinate without reintroducing composition in God.
W7172336769.a2.quote: I conclude by arguing that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but renders theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God‑talk in both metaphysics and the formative practices of religious life.

W7172336769.c001.text: Critics claim that divine simplicity makes God identical to an abstract property and renders theological language vacuous because a simple God cannot ground multiple true intrinsic predicates.
W7172336769.c001.quote: Critics of divine simplicity argue that simplicity renders God identical with an abstract property and/or renders our language about God semantically vacuous since a simple God seems unable to ground a plurality of true intrinsic predicates.

W7172336769.c002.text: The paper aims to defend a broadly Thomistic account of divine simplicity against contemporary metaphysical and semantic objections.
W7172336769.c002.quote: The aim of this paper is to defend a broadly Thomistic account of divine simplicity against a cluster of contemporary metaphysical and semantic objections.

W7172336769.c003.text: The author employs modern analytic philosophy, specifically selected Fregean distinctions, to show how the criticisms of divine simplicity can be defused.
W7172336769.c003.quote: In this paper, I employ the resources of modern analytic philosophy – specifically, selected Fregean distinctions – to demonstrate how these critiques can be defused.

W7172336769.c004.text: This analogical framework supplies principled constraints on theological predication without reintroducing composition into God.
W7172336769.c004.quote: This framework supplies principled constraints on theological predication without reintroducing composition into God.

W7172336769.c005.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but makes theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God‑talk in metaphysics and religious practice.
W7172336769.c005.quote: I conclude by arguing that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but renders theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God‑talk in both metaphysics and the formative practices of religious life.

W7172336769.c006.text: The object‑concept distinction is far less discussed in contemporary literature on divine simplicity than the sense‑reference distinction.
W7172336769.c006.quote: The object/concept distinction, on the other hand, is far less discussed in contemporary literature on divine simplicity.

W7172336769.c007.text: Introducing the object‑concept distinction into Thomistic defenses of simplicity can illuminate the debate and constitute a genuine contribution to those defenses.
W7172336769.c007.quote: This paper argues that bringing this distinction to bear on Thomistic defences of simplicity can be illuminating and make a genuine contribution to these defences.

W7172336769.c008.text: The clarifying procedure using these distinctions, termed Fregean diagnostics, does not yet explain how theological predicates can have truth‑conditions and sufficiently determinate content.
W7172336769.c008.quote: However, the clarifying procedure involving the employment of these distinctions – Fregean diagnostics, as I’ve termed it – does not yet explain how theological predicates can have truth‑conditions and sufficiently determinate content.

W7172336769.c009.text: To address the critics’ underlying concerns, Fregean diagnostics must be located within the broader semantic‑metaphysical framework of the doctrine of analogy.
W7172336769.c009.quote: I argue that in order to address these underlying concerns of the critics of simplicity, Fregean diagnostics must be located in the broader semantic‑metaphysical framework provided by the doctrine of analogy.

W7172336769.c010.text: The analogical framework introduces a further distinction between res significata and modus significandi, providing the resources needed to ground the meaning of theological predicates.
W7172336769.c010.quote: It is this framework that introduces a crucial further distinction that Fregean diagnostics do not give us – namely, the distinction between res significata and modus significandi – and thereby provides the resources needed to ground the meaning of theological predicates.

W7172336769.c011.text: The sense‑reference distinction alone is an incomplete defensive strategy when isolated from the metaphysical framework of analogical semantics.
W7172336769.c011.quote: Thus, this paper contributes to existing debates surrounding simplicity by arguing that the more often‑used sense/reference distinction remains an incomplete defensive strategy if it is isolated from the metaphysical framework of analogical semantics.

W7172336769.c012.text: The object‑concept distinction alone also remains insufficient to ground the meaning of theological predicates.
W7172336769.c012.quote: The same goes for the more rarely used object/concept distinction: it, too, remains insufficient on its own to ground the meaning of theological predicates.

W7172336769.c013.text: The doctrine of divine simplicity denies matter–form composition, the essence–individual distinction, the essence–existence distinction, and the substance–property distinction because God has ontological priority.
W7172336769.c013.quote: More specifically, the doctrine of divine simplicity entails that the following kinds of distinctions and compositions are denied of God due to God’s ontological priority: matter–form composition, the essence–individual distinction, the essence–existence distinction, and the substance–property distinction.

W7172336769.c014.text: According to divine simplicity, God does not have properties; everything God is is all at once in one pure act.
W7172336769.c014.quote: According to the doctrine of divine simplicity, God does not have properties: everything that God is, God is all at once, in one pure act.

W7172336769.c015.text: A distinction between what God is and God’s properties would entail composition, which implies dependence and potentiality, thereby introducing a metaphysical reality prior to God.
W7172336769.c015.quote: A distinction between what God is and God’s properties would entail composition in God. Composition, in turn, implies dependence and potentiality: the whole depends on its parts and the parts could in principle be organised differently.

W7172336769.c016.text: All divine attributes have the same referent, so speaking of God’s goodness or wisdom does not pick out distinct parts in God.
W7172336769.c016.quote: Secondly, it follows that divine attributes all have the same referent: we are not picking out some distinct ‘part’ in God when we speak of God’s goodness, nor yet another when we discuss God’s wisdom.

W7172336769.c017.text: Critics present Conundrum A, concluding that because God is simple and identical with God’s goodness, goodness is God, which would identify God with an abstract property.

W7172336769.c018.text: This would indicate that God isn’t a person but a mere abstract object.
W7172336769.c018.quote: This, in turn, would indicate that God ‘isn’t a person but a mere abstract object’.

W7172336769.c019.text: Thomists hold that God is Life itself and is not a thing, nature, or abstract property, so God can act, know, and will without being a mere abstract object.
W7172336769.c019.quote: God does all these, because God is Life itself. God is not a thing, a nature, or an abstract property.

W7172336769.c020.text: Critics present Conundrum B, arguing that if God is simple, goodness and wisdom become the same thing in God, undermining the meaningfulness of multiple divine attributes.
W7172336769.c020.quote: Therefore, goodness and wisdom are the same thing in God.

W7172336769.c021.text: The doctrine of divine simplicity threatens the coherence and meaningfulness of language about God by rendering multiple divine predicates semantically vacuous.
W7172336769.c021.quote: The doctrine of divine simplicity, therefore, threatens the coherence and meaningfulness of our language about God because it makes it impossible to meaningfully predicate multiple attributes of God.

W7172336769.c022.text: Aquinas possesses a sophisticated semantic‑metaphysical apparatus, based on Fregean sense/reference distinctions, that explains how many names can be predicated of a simple God.
W7172336769.c022.quote: These allow Aquinas to explain how many names can be truly predicated of a simple God.

W7172336769.c023.text: Using Frege’s object/concept distinction we can diagnose the conundrums as semantic misreadings.
W7172336769.c023.quote: My argument is that with the help of Frege’s classic distinction between objects and concepts, we can diagnose these conundrums as semantic misreadings.

W7172336769.c024.text: Fregean distinctions are insufficient for theological predicates, so divine simplicity motivates analogical semantics as a non‑standard but determinate semantic framework.
W7172336769.c024.quote: Fregean distinctions are not sufficient to ground the meaning of theological predicates. Hence, I propose that divine simplicity motivates non-standard but sufficiently determinate semantics, namely analogical semantics.

W7172336769.c025.text: Analogical semantics supplies principled constraints on admissible divine predications, allowing ‘God is good’ while excluding ‘God is evil’ or ‘God is a chair’.
W7172336769.c025.quote: Analogical semantics also supplies principled constraints on admissible divine predications that are grounded in participation and eminence (i.e., it explains why ‘God is good’ is eligible for intrinsic predication while ‘God is evil’ or ‘God is a chair’ is not).

W7172336769.c026.text: Concepts require an object to which they apply; they are parasitic on objects.
W7172336769.c026.quote: to mean something, they need an object. Concepts require something to which they apply; they are parasitic on objects, if you like.

W7172336769.c027.text: Frege distinguishes two kinds of the verb ‘is’: the ‘is’ of predication and the ‘is’ of identification.
W7172336769.c027.quote: Following this, note also Frege’s crucial insight with regard to the word ‘is’, namely, that there are two kinds of ‘is’: the ‘is’ of predication and the ‘is’ of identification.

W7172336769.c028.text: For Aquinas, terms such as ‘goodness’ are abstract perfection terms that can be properly used of God.
W7172336769.c028.quote: Now, for Aquinas, terms such as ‘goodness’ are abstract perfection terms that can be properly used of God.

W7172336769.c029.text: Abstract names denote divine perfections but, given simplicity, they do not denote properties in God or any distinct metaphysical entities; they signify the simple divine being itself under different formal aspects.
W7172336769.c029.quote: Abstract names denote divine perfections but, given simplicity, they do not denote properties in God or any other distinct metaphysical entities. Rather, they signify the simple divine being itself, under different formal aspects.

W7172336769.c030.text: Abstract perfection terms cannot refer to distinct objects in the Fregean sense; they denote the one simple divine being only as concepts.
W7172336769.c030.quote: Abstract perfection terms, therefore, cannot refer to distinct objects in the Fregean sense but rather they denote the one, simple divine being only in the concept sense.

W7172336769.c031.text: In the statement ‘God is good’, ‘good’ is not a thing but a concept predicated of the thing we call God.
W7172336769.c031.quote: Hence, in ‘God is good’, ‘good’ is not ‘a thing’ but rather ‘good’ is a concept predicated of ‘a thing’ we call God.

W7172336769.c032.text: Conundrum A is a semantic confusion that treats ‘God is good’ as equivalent to ‘goodness is God’, mistakenly mixing object‑object with object‑concept predication.
W7172336769.c032.quote: In light of this, we can diagnose Conundrum A as the following kind of confusion: saying that [God is good = goodness is God] is like saying that [the barn is red = red is a barn]. We are confusing object–object predication with object–concept predication.

W7172336769.c033.text: Words such as goodness, divinity, simplicity, or Trinity can be used both in object and concept sense without implying that they are properties in God.
W7172336769.c033.quote: Hence, words like goodness, divinity, simplicity, or Trinity can be used both in object and concept sense, but this does not indicate a shift into the kinds of metaphysics of God, where things such as goodness are properties in God.

W7172336769.c034.text: Critics claim that statements like ‘God is goodness’ and ‘God is wisdom’ are cases of object‑object predication, analogous to ‘the evening star is the planet Venus’.
W7172336769.c034.quote: According to the critics of simplicity, ‘God is goodness’ and ‘God is wisdom’ are akin to (9): they are a case of object–object predication.

W7172336769.c035.text: The fallacy arises from failing to distinguish predication from identification; ‘good’ and ‘wise’ are concepts, not objects, so the inference that God has multiple distinct properties is mistaken.
W7172336769.c035.quote: Logically, the words ‘good’ and ‘wise’ are not objects in (4)–(7) but concepts. This, as I argued, is one of the central semantic results of the doctrine ...

W7172336769.c036.text: Using Frege’s sense‑reference distinction, ‘good’ and ‘wise’ have the same referent—the simple divine being—so multiple attributes are merely different senses of the same object, compatible with divine simplicity.
W7172336769.c036.quote: We can respond to this objection by availing ourselves of another central Fregean distinction, that between sense and reference. ‘Good’ and ‘wise’ both have the same referent: the simple, undivided divine being.

W7172336769.c037.text: The traditional doctrine of divine simplicity denies that God possesses any properties; it does not identify God with properties.
W7172336769.c037.quote: the traditional doctrine of simplicity does not identify God with God’s properties – rather, it denies that God has any properties at all.

W7172336769.c038.text: How can theological predicates have sufficiently determinate content and truth‑conditions if the Fregean distinction alone does not provide a theory of their meaning?
W7172336769.c038.quote: the Fregean distinction does not yet explain how theological predicates can have sufficiently determinate content and truth-conditions.

W7172336769.c039.text: All attempts to ground content without sacrificing divine simplicity, such as minimal truth‑makers, trope theory, property exemplification, and divine attributes as determinables of a super‑property, fail.
W7172336769.c039.quote: all attempts to ground content without sacrificing simplicity (such as minimal truth‑makers, trope theory, property exemplification, divine attributes as determinables of a super‑property) fail.

W7172336769.c040.text: The doctrine of analogy can ground the meaningfulness of theological language without implying any composition in God.
W7172336769.c040.quote: I’ll demonstrate how the doctrine of analogy can ground the meaning­fulness of theological language without implying composition in God.

W7172336769.c041.text: Answering worries about semantic vacuity requires embedding Fregean diagnostics in a broader metaphysical framework, for example analogy.
W7172336769.c041.quote: Answering these worries about meaning requires turning from semantics to metaphysics: Fregean diagnostics must be embedded in a broader metaphysical framework, e.g. analogy.

W7172336769.c042.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy can provide principled constraints and sufficiently determinate content for divine predicates, thereby answering residual worries about meaning.
W7172336769.c042.quote: Our aim in this section is not to rehearse a generic version of the Thomistic doctrine of analogy but to demonstrate how this doctrine can answer the residual worries about meaning from Section 3 by providing principled constraints and sufficiently determinate content for divine predicates.

W7172336769.c043.text: Frege’s distinction between concepts and objects offers a genuine contribution to a Thomistic defence of divine simplicity.
W7172336769.c043.quote: Frege does have something genuinely interesting to contribute to a Thomistic defence of simplicity, namely, his distinction between concepts and objects.

W7172336769.c044.text: Aquinas lacks a Frege‑like sharp logical distinction between complete referential expressions and unsaturated predicative expressions.
W7172336769.c044.quote: Aquinas does, of course, make a distinction between that of which something is predicated and what is being predicated, but he does not quite have a Frege‑like sharp logical distinction between complete referential expressions and unsaturated predicative expressions.

W7172336769.c045.text: The concept/object strategy remains incomplete because it cannot fully address residual worries about the content of theological predicates.
W7172336769.c045.quote: this strategy, like the sense/reference strategy, remains incomplete because it cannot fully address residual worries about the content of theological predicates.

W7172336769.c046.text: To address those worries we must employ Aquinas’s distinction between what is signified (res significata) and the mode of signification (modus significandi).
W7172336769.c046.quote: we must bring in a further distinction from Aquinas that Frege does not have, namely the distinction between what is signified (res significata) and the mode of signification (modus significandi).

W7172336769.c047.text: In God the mode of signifying is creaturely, but what is signified is truly found in God and does not entail any kind of composition.
W7172336769.c047.quote: God, the mode of signifying is creaturely (i.e., speaking of goodness as a property that inheres in an entity), but what is signified (res significata) is truly found in God, except in a metaphysical mode that we cannot properly conceive. We can only say negatively that this mode is not such that it entails any kind of composition.

W7172336769.c048.text: Analogy’s principle holds that creaturely predication, suited to a world of multiplicity, can only speak of God in a creaturely mode, with plurality residing in the mode of signifying, not the signified reality.
W7172336769.c048.quote: Here is also where analogy, in its semantic dimension, finds its originating principle: for creaturely predication is made for a world such as ours – a world of multiplicity and difference – and can, therefore, only speak of God in a creaturely mode. ‘Good’ and ‘wise’ are distinct concepts because our intellect abstracts different aspects from creaturely perfections; in God, there are not distinct aspects but one act.

W7172336769.c049.text: Critics argue that analogy obscures the meaning of terms applied to God because we cannot know whether divine goodness entails the same as human goodness.
W7172336769.c049.quote: analogy obscures the meaning of terms when applied to God: human goodness might, for example, mean that one does not needlessly cause the innocent to suffer, but we have no way of knowing if divine goodness entails the same.

W7172336769.c050.text: Defenders of analogy reply that divine attributes are not entirely senseless; we simply do not know the particular sense in which they obtain in God.
W7172336769.c050.quote: the defenders of analogy would respond to this by arguing that attributes such as ‘love’ are not entirely senseless when applied to God; we just do not know ‘the particular sense in which God’s love, power, or goodness obtain’ with respect to God.

W7172336769.c051.text: The author replies that Misiewicz errs by assuming defenders of analogy cannot specify what makes language about God intelligible.
W7172336769.c051.quote: the thing that leads Misiewicz astray is thinking that the defenders of analogy have no way of specifying what this something is.

W7172336769.c052.text: Much of the confusion about divine simplicity arises from failing to appreciate its apophatic character.
W7172336769.c052.quote: much of the confusion here lies in not appreciating the apophatic character of the classical doctrine of simplicity.

W7172336769.c053.text: Making the relational comparison between creaturely and divine goodness requires putting God in a genus.
W7172336769.c053.quote: Misiewicz says (ibid., pp. 56–60) that making this relational comparison requires putting God in a genus.

W7172336769.c054.text: The reason some think the difference in analogy is unspecified is that they treat the semantic dimension of analogy in isolation from its metaphysical background.
W7172336769.c054.quote: I reckon that the reason Misiewicz, Williams and others think of the difference in analogy as unspecified – a semantic can of worms that opens up the possibility of anything goes predication – is that they treat the semantic dimension of analogy in isolationfromitsmetaphysicalbackground.

W7172336769.c055.text: Analogy is a semantic thesis grounded in the primary metaphysical thesis that creatures participate in perfections pre‑contained in God.
W7172336769.c055.quote: They miss the fact that an analogy is a semantic thesis that is grounded in a primary metaphysical thesis: creatures participate in perfections pre-contained in God.

W7172336769.c056.text: The intelligibility of theological language is grounded because God, as creator, causes all things to reflect Him.
W7172336769.c056.quote: This is the something that grounds the intelligibility of theological language: because God is the creator of all things, all things – to the degree that they have being – reflect God.

W7172336769.c057.text: A fixed metaphysical relation between God and creatures grounds the meaning of analogical predicates and stops semantic regress.
W7172336769.c057.quote: This also puts a stop to the kind of semantic regress Williams worries about: there is a fixed metaphysical relation between God and creatures that grounds the meaning of analogical predicates.

W7172336769.c058.text: Individual entities are not analogies of God; rather, being itself is analogical.
W7172336769.c058.quote: In fact, strictly speaking, it is not the case that individual entities are analogies of God.

W7172336769.c059.text: There can be no analogy between any creaturely entity and a simple God because abstraction by confusion contradicts simplicity.
W7172336769.c059.quote: Thus, there can be no analogy between some creaturely entity X and a simple God.

W7172336769.c060.text: The proportional unity involved in analogy is metaphysical, not arithmetic, and is sui generis because God does not belong to any genus.
W7172336769.c060.quote: the proportional unity is not an arithmetic one but rather a metaphysical one, stemming from God’s causal relationship to creation. It is therefore a sui generis relation – indeed, it is a sui generis relation precisely because God does not belong in any genus.

W7172336769.c061.text: Analogical predication presupposes composition in concepts but not in God; the lack of composition in God makes the predication analogical.
W7172336769.c061.quote: the concepts – and, therefore, analogical predication – presupposes composition, but this does not mean that composition must be read into God in Godself. In fact, it is precisely because there is no composition in God that the predication in question is analogical.

W7172336769.c062.text: For Aquinas, analogy is not merely about causality; God is essentially Good, not just the cause of goodness.
W7172336769.c062.quote: Analogy – for Aquinas, anyways – is not simply a matter of causality.

W7172336769.c063.text: Through analogical reasoning we can know that God would never needlessly cause innocent suffering.
W7172336769.c063.quote: We can therefore know, through analogical reasoning, that God’s goodness means that God would never needlessly cause the innocent to suffer.

W7172336769.c064.text: Only pure perfections can be predicated of God analogically; predicates like ‘God is a chair’ or ‘God can do evil’ are incoherent.
W7172336769.c064.quote: only predicates that signify pure perfections – such as goodness, wisdom, knowledge, being, and life – can be predicated of God analogically since such perfections exist in God eminently and without limitation. By contrast, ‘God is a chair’ involves a category mistake because being a chair entails a material mode of being that God does not have.

W7172336769.c065.text: If God is simple and does not exemplify any property, then all predication about God lacks a subject that makes propositions true.
W7172336769.c065.quote: there is the objection that all predication requires a subject who exemplifies a property. If God is simple and, therefore, does not exemplify a property, then we have no way of predicating anything of God and no way of knowing what is the truth-value of any proposition p in the form of ‘God is X’ because we do not know what in God renders p true.

W7172336769.c066.text: Adopting a truth‑maker view solves the problem: God Himself is the truth‑maker for divine predicates without needing property exemplification.
W7172336769.c066.quote: From the perspective of the truthmaker theory of predication, there is nothing problematic about saying that God is identical with his nature, goodness, power, wisdom, or any other such things.

W7172336769.c067.text: Taking divine simplicity seriously implies that viewing God as an exception to usual truth‑maker functions is expected, not ad hoc.
W7172336769.c067.quote: if we begin from taking divine simplicity seriously, then adopting the view that God provides an exception case for how truth-makers usually function is not adhoc – it is just what we would expect to follow from God’s ontological uniqueness.

W7172336769.c068.text: The objection assumes that every true predication must be classificatory, locating its subject within a genus by attributing an intrinsic feature.
W7172336769.c068.quote: The key mistake in this objection is the assumption that every true predication must be classificatory – i.e., it must locate its subject within a genus by attributing it an intrinsic feature.

W7172336769.c069.text: The concern can be answered by distinguishing intrinsic perfection predication, extrinsic denominations, and metatheoretical role descriptions.
W7172336769.c069.quote: We can answer this concern by distinguishing between intrinsic perfection predication, extrinsic denominations, and metatheoretical role descriptions.

W7172336769.c070.text: Intrinsic perfection predication (e.g., God is good, wise, simple) states what God is in Godself, namely God’s simple essence.
W7172336769.c070.quote: Analogical predication applies to the first of these because intrinsic perfection predication (God is ‘good’, ‘wise’, ‘simple’) involves statements about what God is in Godself – God’s simple essence.

W7172336769.c071.text: Calling God the source of creaturely perfections expresses a metaphysical dependence relation, not an added intrinsic perfection.
W7172336769.c071.quote: To characterise God as the source of creaturely perfections, however, is not to add an additional perfection to God and thereby characterised God’s simple essence as such – it is to simply characterise a metaphysical dependence relation between God and creatures.

W7172336769.c072.text: Saying ‘God is good’ is true because God’s being metaphysically grounds the proposition’s truth, not because it adds an intrinsic predicate.
W7172336769.c072.quote: Similarly, on a truth-maker approach: to say that ‘God is good’ is true is to say that God’s very being is sufficient for (and thus metaphysically grounds) the truth of the proposition.

W7172336769.c073.text: Speaking of God as ‘the truth‑maker of p’ is a metatheoretical role description, not a classificatory predicate.
W7172336769.c073.quote: Thus, to speak of God as ‘the truth-maker of p’ is to speak of God in terms of metatheoretical role descriptions.

W7172336769.c074.text: Critics ask what it actually means to say that God is good.
W7172336769.c074.quote: What, they might ask, does it actually mean to say that God is good?

W7172336769.c075.text: The objection presents a false dichotomy: either a theory fixes theological meanings determinately or it renders them vacuous.
W7172336769.c075.quote: My main issue with this objection is that it involves a false dichotomy: a theological theory of meaning must either be able to provide the semantic tools for determinately fixing the meaning of theological predicates or accept that theological predicates are semantically vacuous.

W7172336769.c076.text: No theological theory can determinately fix meanings because our understanding of predicates like ‘good’ applied to God is always incomplete.
W7172336769.c076.quote: I would like to suggest, however, that it is unlikely that any theological theory of meaning can determinately fix the meaning of theological predicates because our understanding of the meaning of such predicates as ‘good’ when applied to God is always incomplete.

W7172336769.c077.text: A better standard for a theological theory of meaning is to provide grounding for theological meanings that are sufficiently determinate.
W7172336769.c077.quote: Therefore, in my view, a better standard of success for a theological theory of meaning is that our theory should provide theoretical grounding for thinking of theological meanings as sufficiently determinate.

W7172336769.c078.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy can meet the standard of providing sufficiently determinate theological meanings.
W7172336769.c078.quote: I think that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy can meet this standard.

W7172336769.c079.text: Divine simplicity does not make theological language vacuous; it requires a disciplined, analogical mode of predication grounded in participatory metaphysics.
W7172336769.c079.quote: The central claim of this paper, then, has been that divine simplicity does not render theological language vacuous, but instead requires a disciplined, analogical mode of predication grounded in participatory metaphysics.

W7172336769.c080.text: Analogy is a metaphysical doctrine that grounds religious sense‑making practices and cannot be reduced to logical principles.
W7172336769.c080.quote: Analogy ... is a metaphysical doctrine that grounds certain religious practices of sense-making and language-use that cannot be reduced to logical principles.

objections.text: Consider Ruth, a seminary teacher who must grade two essays. Essay A says 'God is wise' and Essay B says 'God is wise in the way a clever chess player is wise.' Ruth applies the framework of res significata and modus significandi: she asks whether the perfection signified (wisdom) is ascribed primarily to God, with creatures possessing it only derivatively. Her rubric instructs her to reward A and penalize B. But when a student, Tomas, asks what 'primarily' means and how the ratio of proportionality between God and creatures is fixed, Ruth can only point to the doctrine's own vocabulary. Her colleague Nadia, a Fregean, asks which sense of 'wise' the rubric fixes, and gets no answer that distinguishes the two essays by truth-conditions. Both teachers agree on grades yet cannot say what each grade tracks. The framework generates verdicts in practice while the semantic content that would ground them remains unspecified, so the claim that analogy is the place where Fregean diagnostics are located does not follow: the analogical framework is invoked to license judgments it does not itself determine.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c009 fails because the analogical framework is asserted as the required host for Fregean diagnostics, yet in the case the framework yields graded verdicts without fixing the determinate sense or reference that the diagnostics need, so it cannot supply the semantic ground it is said to provide.

objections.text: A theologian sets out to defuse the objection that divine simplicity makes God unknowable by deploying modern analytic distinctions between sense and reference on the predicate ‘good’. She claims that ‘good’ has a determinate sense but no distinct reference in God, since God is identical to His essence. During the presentation, a critic presses her: the analytic framework requires predicates to denote concepts under which objects fall, and objects must be distinct from the concepts they instantiate. If God is absolutely simple, there is no gap between object and concept in Him; treating God as an object that falls under a concept reintroduces metaphysical complexity. The theologian’s tools therefore cannot map onto divine simplicity without collapsing the doctrine into a standard property–substance ontology. The original worry—that simplicity strips God of any content we could grasp—remains untouched because the semantic framework was never equipped to handle a being that is pure act with no composition. The employment of these distinctions fails to defuse the criticism.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c003 fails because deploying modern analytic sense–reference distinctions to defuse criticisms of divine simplicity presupposes a subject–property complexity that the doctrine explicitly rejects, leaving the original criticism fully intact.

objections.text: Two medieval theologians, Brother A and Brother B, both committed to the Thomistic analogical framework, predicate 'God is good' of God. Both accept that divine goodness analogically exceeds created goodness in an eminent, unlimited way—this is the constraint the framework supplies. Yet Brother A concludes that God's eminent goodness entails universal salvation, since a perfectly good being would not permit eternal damnation. Brother B concludes that God's eminent goodness entails just punishment, since a perfectly good being would not ignore justice. Each invokes the same analogical rule—'God is good in an eminent, unlimited way'—to reach opposite conclusions about what divine goodness actually requires. The framework excludes 'God is evil' but provides no determinate content deciding whether divine goodness includes mercy over justice or justice over mercy. The analogy tells them God's goodness exceeds ours, but not in which specific respects, leaving the predicate's content underdetermined for doctrinal and practical disputes.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c042 fails because the Thomistic doctrine of analogy supplies exclusionary constraints but not sufficiently determinate content, as shown by two theologians reaching contradictory substantive conclusions from the same analogical predicate.

objections.text: A medieval monk, using ‘God is a lion’ in a sermon, intends the symbolism of strength and sovereignty. The congregation understands it as a pious metaphor, not a literal or ontological claim. Yet, under analogical semantics, ‘lion’ is not a standard divine predicate, nor does it fit the constraints that exclude ‘God is a chair’. The phrase is meaningful in practice but violates the premise’s claim that analogical semantics *principled* constraints exclude all non-admissible predications.
objections.premise_fails_because: c025 fails because analogical semantics does not exclude all non-theological predicates (e.g., ‘lion’) that are meaningfully used in religious practice.

objections.text: A parish priest, Father Maren, must preach on 'God is one.' He applies the res/modus distinction: the modus significandi ('X is one') is identical in 'God is one' and 'a rowing team is one'; the res significata differs (divine oneness vs. team unity). He now asks what divine oneness consists in—simplicity, absence of composition, unity of attributes? The distinction tells him only that the res differs from team unity. It labels a gap. It offers no criterion for filling the res significata slot with determinate content. Maren cannot move from 'God is one, differently from a team is one' to any positive account of what divine oneness is. The modus is fixed; the res remains a placeholder the framework itself cannot populate. Without a fill, no predicate is grounded; only its indeterminacy is named. The distinction sorts predicates into 'divine' and 'human' slots but supplies nothing that makes the divine slot meaningful rather than merely labeled.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c010 fails because the res significata / modus significandi distinction merely marks that theological and human predicates differ in what they signify while sharing a mode of expression, but it provides no mechanism for determining the content of the theological res significata, leaving it an empty placeholder that cannot ground meaning rather than merely flagging indeterminacy.

objections.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who uses the Thomistic doctrine of analogy to interpret divine predicates. She believes that 'God is good' has a determinate meaning, but her interpretation relies on a complex web of metaphysical assumptions. In practice, Emma's community has varying understandings of 'good', leading to disagreements about God's nature. Despite the doctrine's constraints, the community's diverse perspectives on divine goodness persist, indicating that determinacy in theological language is not solely due to the doctrine's supplies.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that the determinacy supplied by the Thomistic doctrine of analogy is sufficient to answer worries about meaning, when in fact, the complexities of human interpretation and the persistence of diverse perspectives can undermine such determinacy.

objections.text: Consider the monk Ioannis of a remote monastery. He receives the uncreated divine energies in the Divine Liturgy, experiencing God’s love, wisdom, and power as living realities, not as merely semantic predicates. A philosopher using the analogical framework would say the rule “allow ‘God is good’ but exclude ‘God is a chair’” secures meaning. Yet Ioannis knows that calling God a chair is barred because the divine energies cannot be reduced to any created category, not because of a linguistic constraint. The same reason that permits “God is love” is the participation in the uncreated energy of love, which transcends any analogical semantic scheme. Thus the premise that analogical semantics alone supplies the principled exclusion fails to account for the essence‑energies distinction that truly governs divine predication.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c025 fails because analogical semantics alone cannot determine admissible divine predications; the true constraints come from the Eastern Orthodox distinction between God's essence and uncreated energies.

objections.text: A theologian believes that because analogy provides "sufficiently determinate content," the predicate "wise" and the predicate "good" correspond to distinct, determinate metaphysical specifications within the divine essence. Consequently, they treat God as a composite of these distinct specifications. This view forces a composition upon God, transforming the single, undivided Act of Being into a collection of distinct, determinate properties. By attempting to secure semantic determinacy, the theologian inadvertently destroys divine simplicity, which requires that God be absolutely without parts or multiplicity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c042 fails because "sufficiently determinate content" implies a multiplicity of distinct metaphysical specifications that would violate the principle of divine simplicity.

objections.text: A semantic theorist argues that for a predicate to carry determinate content, there must be a fixed and exhaustive relationship between the signifier and the signified. The doctrine of analogy, by design, preserves 'semantic openness,' meaning the relationship between the human term and the divine reality is intentionally left under-specified. If this relationship is under-specified, the 'content' provided by analogy consists only of negative constraints—limiting what the term cannot mean—without providing the positive, specific information required for determinacy. Consequently, the openness that the argument seeks to preserve prevents the term from actually possessing the determinate content necessary for meaningful predication.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c042 fails because semantic openness and sufficiently determinate content are mutually exclusive.

objections.text: Consider Ruth, a preacher in a rural congregation, who tells her flock that God is 'good' and, when asked what this means, answers: 'God is not like the good things we see, which come mixed with defect; God's goodness is the source of all goodness, and far exceeds it.' Her hearers leave with a usable sense: do not treat God's goodness as a quality that could be lost, outweighed, or matched by a rival. Now a parishioner, Tom, asks whether God's goodness might be compatible with God permitting a child's suffering for reasons God alone knows. Ruth's framework offers only negation and eminence: God is not defective, and God's goodness exceeds our notion. It yields no verdict. Tom cannot decide whether to trust God in his grief, nor what a 'good' God would or would not do. The negations exclude defect but leave every positive question about divine action open. The worry about meaning arises precisely at the point where practice requires positive content, and eminence only restates that content is beyond reach.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise arg1.r1 claims negation and eminence supply determinate positive content sufficient for practice, but in Ruth's case they exclude only defect and cannot settle the practical question Tom faces, so the determinacy claimed is not delivered.

objections.text: A parish council must decide whether to shelter refugees. They ask their pastor whether God commands hospitality. Under the Thomistic analogical framework, 'hospitable' is deemed admissible and said primarily of God, while 'cruel' is excluded. Yet the framework assigns no truth-conditional sense to 'God is hospitable': it does not specify whether divine hospitality welcomes all strangers unconditionally or only the righteous. Because the council cannot derive any actionable content from the predicate beyond its bare label, they remain unable to decide whether turning families away violates God's nature. The formal constraint on admissible words therefore fails to guide practice; without at least partial truth-conditional content, the distinction between primary and derivative predication collapses into a mere lexical permission list. The promised determinacy for practice is illusory.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.arg1.r2 fails because purely formal constraints on admissible predicates without truth-conditional sense are too thin to resolve concrete practical questions, so theological language is not in fact constrained enough for practice.

objections.text: Two Thomist theologians, both trained in the analogical framework with its res significata/modus significandi distinction, disagree about whether 'God suffers' is a legitimate predication. The first argues that suffering, as the patient's proper response to love's rejection, is said analogically of God: the res significata (loving endurance of evil) is properly divine, only the modus significandi (passive reception) is creaturely. He concludes that a pastoral worker should tell a grieving mother that God truly shares her pain. The second theologian, using the same framework, insists that suffering involves potency and composition, which are contrary to what is said primarily of God—simplicity and impassibility—so the predication must be excluded entirely, and the pastoral worker should instead say that God is present to her suffering without himself suffering. Both reason within the analogical framework; neither violates its stated constraints. The framework provides no principled mechanism for deciding which of these predications is 'contrary to what is said primarily of God,' because that determination itself depends on prior, non-analogically-settled judgments about which divine attributes are primary.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.arg1.r3 fails because the analogical framework's constraints cannot rule out predications contrary to what is said primarily of God when theologians using those very constraints reach opposite verdicts on the same predication, showing the constraints are not principled enough to exclude clearly unacceptable practical verdicts.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that the rule permitting 'God is good' and excluding 'God is a chair' is not grounded in analogical semantics (res significata/modus significandi constraints) but in the essence-energies distinction: the exclusion holds because the uncreated divine energies cannot be reduced to any created category, so the principled constraint on divine predication is metaphysical-participatory rather than semantic, and the analogical scheme therefore fails to supply the operative determinacy.
restatements.plain_english: The rule that lets us say 'God is good' but not 'God is a chair' is not really a rule about words. We exclude 'chair' because God cannot be squeezed into any category of created things, and we allow 'love' because we actually share in God's living love. So the real reason for the limits lies in what God is and how we take part in God, not in a set of linguistic rules, and a theory of meaning alone cannot explain the limits.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the philosophy of religion, this is an objection from religious experience and grounding: the constraints on predicating attributes of God are secured by an experiential or participatory relation to the divine (a non-inferential acquaintance with God's gifts), not by a semantic theory of predication. Compare the claim in Reformed epistemology and mystical theology that the ground of religious language lies in acquaintance, so that a purely semantic account of divine predication leaves the real constraint unexplained.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy cannot supply determinate content for divine predicates: because analogy deliberately preserves semantic openness, the relation between the res significata and the divine reality stays under-specified, so the analogy yields only negative constraints (what the term cannot mean) and no positive, exhaustive signification, which determinacy of predication requires.
restatements.plain_english: Saying a word has a clear meaning requires that it be tied exactly and completely to what it refers to. The approach that says God-talk works by similarity keeps that tie loose on purpose. So all it can tell us is what a word cannot mean about God, not what it does mean, and without a positive meaning the words cannot really say anything determinate about God.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the debate over religious language and apophatic theology, this is the charge that analogical or negative predication leaves divine attributes semantically empty: a via negativa that only excludes and never affirms, so that talk of God's goodness has no determinate truth-conditions. It parallels the univocity-versus-equivocity dilemma pressed by Scotus and later critics of analogy, and the verificationist and cognitivist worry that predicates without fixed reference cannot be meaningful.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy, by relying on negation (removing defect from God's goodness) and eminence (God's goodness exceeds and grounds creaturely goodness), yields only the exclusion of defect and not the positive content that practical questions require: a res significata of 'goodness' fixed well enough to settle whether God's permitting a child's suffering is compatible with divine goodness, so the determinacy the framework claims is insufficient at exactly the point where the modus significandi must bear practical weight.
restatements.plain_english: Saying God is good only by ruling out flaws and saying God's goodness is greater than ours doesn't tell a worried person what a good God would or wouldn't do. So when someone asks whether God's goodness fits with a child suffering, this way of talking gives no answer, and the meaning people need for trusting God in grief is missing.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the problem of evil and the epistemology of religious testimony, this is an argument that apophatic or via-negativa theism is practically idle: the 'skeptical theist' retreat to God's inscrutable reasons, reinforced by negative and eminent attributes alone, leaves the hearer without the positive evaluative content needed to judge divine action, so the view fails the test of usable belief for a believer facing suffering.

So if a church asks whether God wants them to take in refugees, a rule that says 'hospitable' is an acceptable word for God doesn't answer the question. The rule only lists allowed words; it doesn't say what they require, so it can't settle what to do.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection holds that the analogical framework, with its res significata/modus significandi distinction and its principle that predicates are said primarily of God, fails to decide contested predications such as 'God suffers' when two competent analogists reason correctly within it, because which attributes count as primary (e.g. impassibility versus loving endurance as res significata) is settled by prior judgments outside the analogical semantics, so the framework cannot by itself ground the exclusion of contrary predications.
restatements.plain_english: Two people who both follow the same set of rules for talking about God can reach opposite answers on whether 'God suffers' is allowed. The rules say what must not be said about God, but they don't say which of God's qualities count as the most basic ones, and that is the very question that decides this case. So the rules alone can't settle it; something else has to.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: Like the epistemology of disagreement, where equally competent peers who share the same evidence and method still split on a verdict, this objection says that a shared inferential framework (here the analogy of being, with its ranking of divine attributes) underdetermines the verdict in a contested case. The ranking of which attributes are basic is a prior, extra-framework commitment, so the framework fails to adjudicate hard cases such as whether God suffers, as in debates over divine passibility in the problem-of-evil and theodicy literature.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks c010's claim that the res/modus distinction provides 'the resources needed to ground the meaning of theological predicates.' It argues that the distinction merely labels a gap between divine and human predication without supplying any criterion for filling the res significata with determinate content. This is a straightforward attack on the premise as stated: c010 says the distinction provides grounding resources; the objection says it does not. Whether the objection succeeds is not for the Referee to decide, but it engages exactly with what c010 claims.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the res/modus distinction, taken by itself, sorts predicates and names a gap, and Maren cannot read off from 'God is one, differently from a team is one' what divine oneness consists in. The argument never claims otherwise. Its claim in c010 is that the distinction is one resource in a framework, and c005 places the determinacy in metaphysics and religious practice. Your objection therefore lands on c010 as worded, but not on c005 as a whole. The open question c038 already flags the same gap, and I accept that the text leaves the fill underspecified.

Still, the objection overstates what a fill requires. Aquinas does not fill the res slot by a definition of divine oneness; he fills it by a set of denial-and-eminence moves and by the via negativa that the Triplex Via literature treats as fixing the referent of 'God' [W4206101892.a2]. Maren can say that divine oneness is whatever is signified by 'one' with the composition-excluding negations applied, which excludes some candidate contents (a team's unity of parts, a composite whole) while leaving the positive content analogically open. That is a criterion, if a thin one. The Dominus Deus Noster reading [W4399543962.a1] shows the unity-versus-plurality question has determinate sense for Aquinas even when its full content is not spelled out.

So I think the objection shows c010 needs more than the distinction. The argument survives only if we add a premise that the analogical framework includes a determination procedure (negation plus eminence plus practice) that yields content excluding some candidates, not merely a labeled slot.
rounds.revised_premise: The Thomistic analogical framework includes a determination procedure (negation of composition plus eminence applied to the signified perfection, anchored in religious practice) that excludes some candidate contents for divine predicates, so the res significata slot receives thin but non-empty determinate content.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede c010 needs more, yet you rescue the argument by calling negation-and-eminence "a criterion, if a thin one." That thinness is the problem. Maren asks what divine oneness consists in. You answer: whatever "one" signifies with composition-excluding negations applied. But that tells him only what divine oneness is not—not composed, not a team's unity. He is left with "highest form," but highest form among what remaining candidates? Negation narrows a set; eminence points upward from it. Neither says whether divine oneness is simplicity, absence of composition, or unity of attributes. The framework moves from a labeled placeholder to a narrower placeholder. For a priest who must preach, exclusion is not determination. Your added premise saves the argument only if "sufficiently determinate" means "not every candidate survives," not "the priest knows what to say." Those are different standards, and c005 commits to the second.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the res/modus distinction alone sorts predicates and names a gap, and c010 as worded claims only that it provides 'the resources' to ground meaning. But your rejoinder runs two standards together, and I want to separate them. Exclusion narrows; it does not fill. I concede that. Still, Aquinas's own practice treats 'one' as having content through the via negativa and eminence together, not through a definition of divine oneness [W4206101892.a2]. Maren can preach that God is one in the sense that God is not divided into parts, not a composite of essence and existence, and not one among many, and that this unity is the source of all creaturely unity. Those are positive claims about the res, and the priest can say them. What he cannot do is give a complete account of the res, and no theist's account of divine simplicity offers one. The open question in c038 concerns exactly this completeness gap, and the argument's own c005 claims 'sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice', which I read as the second standard, not the first. I take that as a real weakness: the argument does not establish that a priest knows what to say in full, only that he has determinate, if partial, content. I hold that the weaker standard is the one that matters for meaning, since meaning does not require complete specification.

Revised premise: The Thomistic framework supplies, via negation and eminence, determinate positive content for divine predicates sufficient for meaningful preaching and practice, though not a complete specification of the res significata.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that the bare distinction does not by itself tell Father Maren what divine oneness positively consists in—it marks a formal gap. But the argument never claims the distinction alone performs that task; it introduces the distinction as a further resource within the broader analogical framework [W7172336769.c009], and the text explicitly acknowledges that the Fregean distinction alone does not provide a theory of meaning [W7172336769.c038]. The determinate content comes from the doctrine of analogy as a whole, which supplies principled constraints on admissible predications [W7172336769.c025], and from the fixed referent for 'God' that allows an intelligible account of divinity [W4206101892.a2]. The res significata is therefore not an empty placeholder: knowing that God is not composite and is the source of unity gives Maren genuinely constrained, if semantically open, content. The distinction sorts the predicate into its proper analogical mode; the broader framework fills the divine slot. So the framework does populate the res significata, but only when the distinction is read as operating within that larger semantic-metaphysical structure.

Revised premise: The res/modus distinction is a necessary formal tool within the analogical framework, yet the determinate content of the res significata is supplied by the broader metaphysical context—particularly the fixed referent of 'God' and the principled constraints of analogy—rather than by the distinction itself.

You are right that the framework, as stated, is invoked to license verdicts (Ruth's rubric) without fixing the sense of 'wise', and that c009 by itself does not show analogy determines truth-conditions. But your example conflates two things the argument separates: the determinacy of the predicate's content and the determinacy of the grade. The argument's claim (c005, c025) is that analogy constrains which predications are admissible, not that it delivers a Fregean sense for each. Ruth's inability to say what 'primarily' means is a failure of exposition, not evidence that the constraint is empty; the res significata/modus significandi distinction [W7172336769.c010] does give a principled asymmetry, since perfection is said of God in its own mode and of creatures derivatively, and that asymmetry is what separates A from B. Where I must concede is the step from that asymmetry to 'sufficiently determinate content'. The metaphysical grounding [W7172336769.c057] fixes the reference of analogical predicates only if the participation relation is itself specified, and the argument does not yet specify it in a way that yields truth-conditions distinguishing 'wise' from 'wise as a chess player'. Its own reference move [W7172336769.c036] works only for the simple divine referent, not for the proportionality ratio that Tomas asks about. So the framework licenses constraints and practice, but the Fregean-style content your objection demands is not supplied, and the 'determinacy' in c005 is overstated.

rounds.content: You press a real worry: if Ruth can only gesture at 'primary' analogy, the framework risks circularity. But you treat analogy as a purely semantic device, whereas the argument presents it as a semantic thesis grounded in the metaphysical relation that creatures participate in perfections pre-contained in God [W7172336769.c055]. That metaphysics fixes the truth-conditions: intrinsic perfection predication states what God is in Godself, so Essay A is true because wisdom is God's simple essence, while Essay B falsely imposes a creaturely mode [W7172336769.c070]. Nadia's Fregean concern is addressed by locating sense in the modus significandi determined by this metaphysics: multiple attributes are different senses of the same simple referent [W7172336769.c036], and the relation stops regress [W7172336769.c057]. You are right that the semantic vocabulary alone does not specify content; the argument survives only because the semantic is inseparable from the metaphysical grounding [W7172336769.c009]. Semantic openness remains [W7172336769.c005], but the content is sufficiently determinate because it is metaphysically fixed, not lexically opaque.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
Your reply moves the determinacy from the lexicon into metaphysics, but it does not show that the metaphysics is available to Ruth as a criterion. Ruth's rubric must sort Essay A from Essay B. You say the truth-conditions are fixed because wisdom is God's simple essence and Essay B "falsely imposes a creaturely mode." Yet that verdict requires knowing which mode is God's and which is creaturely, and that is exactly what Tomas asked her to specify. Appealing to the metaphysical grounding relocates the question about the ratio of proportionality; it does not answer it.

Nor does the claim that multiple attributes are different senses of one simple referent help Nadia's question. If "wise" in Essay A and "wise" in Essay B both pick out the one simple essence, then the two essays do not differ in truth-value by reference, and you still owe a sense-level difference that Ruth can apply. Pointing to the modus significandi repeats the problem one level down.

So I grant that the metaphysics would fix content if it were independently determinate. The objection stands unless you can show that Ruth, without already knowing the answer, can apply it to distinguish A from B.

rounds.content:
You press a genuine gap. But you are right that ontological determination is not operational determination: Ruth can formally exclude creaturely modes, yet the positive sense of 'wise' in Essay A remains specified only by negation and metaphysical participation, not by a Fregean sense she can independently articulate. The argument conflates metaphysical truth-making with practical criterion-giving. I concede that the argument as stated does not survive your challenge. To save it, one must add that the res significata/modus significandi distinction yields a practically applicable formal rule—exclude creaturely modes—so that competent practitioners can judge predications correctly even when the positive divine modus exceeds complete lexical specification.

rounds.content:
You are right that r2 concedes the absence of truth-conditional sense for each predicate, so the argument never promised that 'God is hospitable' settles whether to shelter families. Its claim is narrower: the framework fixes which predicates are said primarily of God and which derivatively, and that is enough for practice in the sense that a community can rule out predications that would contradict the admitted ones (for example, that God's hospitality is cruel), while leaving the finer question open. The pastor can say that turning away the destitute stranger is at odds with what is said primarily of God, even without a full specification of the res significata [W7172336769.c004][W7172336769.c025]. Still, your point lands on the conclusion: 'sufficiently determinate for practice' overstates what a constraint-only framework delivers. A permission list that excludes 'cruel' does guide action in cases where the act is plainly cruel, but it is silent on the borderline case you describe, and the author's own open question concedes that determinate truth-conditions are not yet supplied [W7172336769.c038]. So the argument survives only as a weaker claim: constraint for practice, not determinacy sufficient to decide hard cases. I concede that the conclusion as worded, and the 'practice' claim in r2, must be narrowed.

The argument explicitly claims the framework is 'constrained enough for practice' (arg1.r2) and provides content 'sufficient for meaningful preaching and practice' (arg1.r1). The objection challenges this sufficiency by showing that two theologians operating within the same analogical framework reach opposite practical conclusions about what divine goodness requires, arguing the content is 'underdetermined for doctrinal and practical disputes.' rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the framework, as the objection describes it, fixes only that God's goodness is said primarily and eminently, and does not by itself settle whether mercy or justice is weightier. But the argument never claimed that analogy determines the doctrinal verdict. Its revised premise r1 says the framework supplies determinate content 'sufficient for meaningful preaching and practice, though not a complete specification,' and r2 says it constrains which predications are primary and which derivative while leaving 'semantic openness about its precise content.' Brother A and Brother B's disagreement is exactly the openness the argument already concedes. The disagreement does show something, though: the constraint excludes 'God is evil' and 'God is a chair' [W7172336769.c025], but it does not adjudicate between two admissible, eminent goodnesses. So the dispute is a live test of whether 'sufficient for practice' has teeth. I think it does, in one respect: both brothers are forced to reason from a shared picture of goodness as ordered toward the divine good, which is the sense in which the doctrine ties meaning to metaphysics rather than to free stipulation. Yet that is a constraint on the reasoning, not a verdict. I concede the argument as stated overreaches if c042 is read as claiming determinacy sufficient to resolve doctrinal disputes; the defensible claim is narrower, and the objection shows that narrower claim is all the framework can bear.

Their dispute stems from extra premises about freedom and justice, not from a semantic vacuum in 'God is good'. objection.text: Consider Ruth, a seminary teacher who must grade two essays. Essay A says 'God is wise' and Essay B says 'God is wise in the way a clever chess player is wise.' Ruth applies the framework of res significata and modus significandi: she asks whether the perfection signified (wisdom) is ascribed primarily to God, with creatures possessing it only derivatively. Her rubric instructs her to reward A and penalize B. But when a student, Tomas, asks what 'primarily' means and how the ratio of proportionality between God and creatures is fixed, Ruth can only point to the doctrine's own vocabulary. Her colleague Nadia, a Fregean, asks which sense of 'wise' the rubric fixes, and gets no answer that distinguishes the two essays by truth-conditions. Both teachers agree on grades yet cannot say what each grade tracks. The framework generates verdicts in practice while the semantic content that would ground them remains unspecified, so the claim that analogy is the place where Fregean diagnostics are located does not follow: the analogical framework is invoked to license judgments it does not itself determine.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c009 fails because the analogical framework is asserted as the required host for Fregean diagnostics, yet in the case the framework yields graded verdicts without fixing the determinate sense or reference that the diagnostics need, so it cannot supply the semantic ground it is said to provide.

objection.text: A theologian sets out to defuse the objection that divine simplicity makes God unknowable by deploying modern analytic distinctions between sense and reference on the predicate ‘good’. She claims that ‘good’ has a determinate sense but no distinct reference in God, since God is identical to His essence. During the presentation, a critic presses her: the analytic framework requires predicates to denote concepts under which objects fall, and objects must be distinct from the concepts they instantiate. If God is absolutely simple, there is no gap between object and concept in Him; treating God as an object that falls under a concept reintroduces metaphysical complexity. The theologian’s tools therefore cannot map onto divine simplicity without collapsing the doctrine into a standard property–substance ontology. The original worry—that simplicity strips God of any content we could grasp—remains untouched because the semantic framework was never equipped to handle a being that is pure act with no composition. The employment of these distinctions fails to defuse the criticism.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c003 fails because deploying modern analytic sense–reference distinctions to defuse criticisms of divine simplicity presupposes a subject–property complexity that the doctrine explicitly rejects, leaving the original criticism fully intact.

objection.text: Two medieval theologians, Brother A and Brother B, both committed to the Thomistic analogical framework, predicate 'God is good' of God. Both accept that divine goodness analogically exceeds created goodness in an eminent, unlimited way—this is the constraint the framework supplies. Yet Brother A concludes that God's eminent goodness entails universal salvation, since a perfectly good being would not permit eternal damnation. Brother B concludes that God's eminent goodness entails just punishment, since a perfectly good being would not ignore justice. Each invokes the same analogical rule—'God is good in an eminent, unlimited way'—to reach opposite conclusions about what divine goodness actually requires. The framework excludes 'God is evil' but provides no determinate content deciding whether divine goodness includes mercy over justice or justice over mercy. The analogy tells them God's goodness exceeds ours, but not in which specific respects, leaving the predicate's content underdetermined for doctrinal and practical disputes.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c042 fails because the Thomistic doctrine of analogy supplies exclusionary constraints but not sufficiently determinate content, as shown by two theologians reaching contradictory substantive conclusions from the same analogical predicate.

objection.text: A medieval monk, using ‘God is a lion’ in a sermon, intends the symbolism of strength and sovereignty. The congregation understands it as a pious metaphor, not a literal or ontological claim. Yet, under analogical semantics, ‘lion’ is not a standard divine predicate, nor does it fit the constraints that exclude ‘God is a chair’. The phrase is meaningful in practice but violates the premise’s claim that analogical semantics *principled* constraints exclude all non-admissible predications.
objection.premise_fails_because: c025 fails because analogical semantics does not exclude all non-theological predicates (e.g., ‘lion’) that are meaningfully used in religious practice.

objection.text: A parish priest, Father Maren, must preach on 'God is one.' He applies the res/modus distinction: the modus significandi ('X is one') is identical in 'God is one' and 'a rowing team is one'; the res significata differs (divine oneness vs. team unity). He now asks what divine oneness consists in—simplicity, absence of composition, unity of attributes? The distinction tells him only that the res differs from team unity. It labels a gap. It offers no criterion for filling the res significata slot with determinate content. Maren cannot move from 'God is one, differently from a team is one' to any positive account of what divine oneness is. The modus is fixed; the res remains a placeholder the framework itself cannot populate. Without a fill, no predicate is grounded; only its indeterminacy is named. The distinction sorts predicates into 'divine' and 'human' slots but supplies nothing that makes the divine slot meaningful rather than merely labeled.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c010 fails because the res significata / modus significandi distinction merely marks that theological and human predicates differ in what they signify while sharing a mode of expression, but it provides no mechanism for determining the content of the theological res significata, leaving it an empty placeholder that cannot ground meaning rather than merely flagging indeterminacy.

objection.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who uses the Thomistic doctrine of analogy to interpret divine predicates. She believes that 'God is good' has a determinate meaning, but her interpretation relies on a complex web of metaphysical assumptions. In practice, Emma's community has varying understandings of 'good', leading to disagreements about God's nature. Despite the doctrine's constraints, the community's diverse perspectives on divine goodness persist, indicating that determinacy in theological language is not solely due to the doctrine's supplies.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that the determinacy supplied by the Thomistic doctrine of analogy is sufficient to answer worries about meaning, when in fact, the complexities of human interpretation and the persistence of diverse perspectives can undermine such determinacy.

objection.text: Consider the monk Ioannis of a remote monastery. He receives the uncreated divine energies in the Divine Liturgy, experiencing God’s love, wisdom, and power as living realities, not as merely semantic predicates. A philosopher using the analogical framework would say the rule “allow ‘God is good’ but exclude ‘God is a chair’” secures meaning. Yet Ioannis knows that calling God a chair is barred because the divine energies cannot be reduced to any created category, not because of a linguistic constraint. The same reason that permits “God is love” is the participation in the uncreated energy of love, which transcends any analogical semantic scheme. Thus the premise that analogical semantics alone supplies the principled exclusion fails to account for the essence‑energies distinction that truly governs divine predication.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W7172336769.c025 fails because analogical semantics alone cannot determine admissible divine predications; the true constraints come from the Eastern Orthodox distinction between God's essence and uncreated energies.

objection.text: A theologian believes that because analogy provides "sufficiently determinate content," the predicate "wise" and the predicate "good" correspond to distinct, determinate metaphysical specifications within the divine essence. Consequently, they treat God as a composite of these distinct specifications. This view forces a composition upon God, transforming the single, undivided Act of Being into a collection of distinct, determinate properties. By attempting to secure semantic determinacy, the theologian inadvertently destroys divine simplicity, which requires that God be absolutely without parts or multiplicity.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c042 fails because "sufficiently determinate content" implies a multiplicity of distinct metaphysical specifications that would violate the principle of divine simplicity.

objection.text: A semantic theorist argues that for a predicate to carry determinate content, there must be a fixed and exhaustive relationship between the signifier and the signified. The doctrine of analogy, by design, preserves 'semantic openness,' meaning the relationship between the human term and the divine reality is intentionally left under-specified. If this relationship is under-specified, the 'content' provided by analogy consists only of negative constraints—limiting what the term cannot mean—without providing the positive, specific information required for determinacy. Consequently, the openness that the argument seeks to preserve prevents the term from actually possessing the determinate content necessary for meaningful predication.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7172336769.c042 fails because semantic openness and sufficiently determinate content are mutually exclusive.

turn.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks W7172336769.c009's claim that Fregean diagnostics must be located within the framework of the doctrine of analogy. It argues that the analogical framework (with its res significata / modus significandi distinction) generates practical verdicts without specifying the semantic content that would ground them, and therefore does not earn its role as the broader framework for Fregean diagnostics. This is a direct challenge to the premise as stated, not an attack on something the argument does not claim.

turn.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks c010's claim that the res/modus distinction provides 'the resources needed to ground the meaning of theological predicates.' It argues that the distinction merely labels a gap between divine and human predication without supplying any criterion for filling the res significata with determinate content. This is a straightforward attack on the premise as stated: c010 says the distinction provides grounding resources; the objection says it does not. turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that the framework, as stated, is invoked to license verdicts (Ruth's rubric) without fixing the sense of 'wise', and that c009 by itself does not show analogy determines truth-conditions. But your example conflates two things the argument separates: the determinacy of the predicate's content and the determinacy of the grade. The argument's claim (c005, c025) is that analogy constrains which predications are admissible, not that it delivers a Fregean sense for each. Ruth's inability to say what 'primarily' means is a failure of exposition, not evidence that the constraint is empty; the res significata/modus significandi distinction [W7172336769.c010] does give a principled asymmetry, since perfection is said of God in its own mode and of creatures derivatively, and that asymmetry is what separates A from B. Where I must concede is the step from that asymmetry to 'sufficiently determinate content'. The metaphysical grounding [W7172336769.c057] fixes the reference of analogical predicates only if the participation relation is itself specified, and the argument does not yet specify it in a way that yields truth-conditions distinguishing 'wise' from 'wise as a chess player'. Its own reference move [W7172336769.c036] works only for the simple divine referent, not for the proportionality ratio that Tomas asks about. So the framework licenses constraints and practice, but the Fregean-style content your objection demands is not supplied, and the 'determinacy' in c005 is overstated.

Revised premise: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy supplies principled constraints on admissible divine predications (determining which predicates are said primarily of God and which derivatively), but not truth-conditional sense for each predicate, so the claim is that theological language is constrained enough for practice while semantic openness about its precise content remains.
