turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that the res/modus distinction, taken by itself, sorts predicates and names a gap, and Maren cannot read off from 'God is one, differently from a team is one' what divine oneness consists in. The argument never claims otherwise. Its claim in c010 is that the distinction is one resource in a framework, and c005 places the determinacy in metaphysics and religious practice. Your objection therefore lands on c010 as worded, but not on c005 as a whole. The open question c038 already flags the same gap, and I accept that the text leaves the fill underspecified.

Still, the objection overstates what a fill requires. Aquinas does not fill the res slot by a definition of divine oneness; he fills it by a set of denial-and-eminence moves and by the via negativa that the Triplex Via literature treats as fixing the referent of 'God' [W4206101892.a2]. Maren can say that divine oneness is whatever is signified by 'one' with the composition-excluding negations applied, which excludes some candidate contents (a team's unity of parts, a composite whole) while leaving the positive content analogically open. That is a criterion, if a thin one. The Dominus Deus Noster reading [W4399543962.a1] shows the unity-versus-plurality question has determinate sense for Aquinas even when its full content is not spelled out.

So I think the objection shows c010 needs more than the distinction. The argument survives only if we add a premise that the analogical framework includes a determination procedure (negation plus eminence plus practice) that yields content excluding some candidates, not merely a labeled slot.
turn.revised_premise: The Thomistic analogical framework includes a determination procedure (negation of composition plus eminence applied to the signified perfection, anchored in religious practice) that excludes some candidate contents for divine predicates, so the res significata slot receives thin but non-empty determinate content.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content: You concede c010 needs more, yet you rescue the argument by calling negation-and-eminence "a criterion, if a thin one." That thinness is the problem. Maren asks what divine oneness consists in. You answer: whatever "one" signifies with composition-excluding negations applied. But that tells him only what divine oneness is not—not composed, not a team's unity. He is left with "highest form," but highest form among what remaining candidates? Negation narrows a set; eminence points upward from it. Neither says whether divine oneness is simplicity, absence of composition, or unity of attributes. The framework moves from a labeled placeholder to a narrower placeholder. For a priest who must preach, exclusion is not determination. Your added premise saves the argument only if "sufficiently determinate" means "not every candidate survives," not "the priest knows what to say." Those are different standards, and c005 commits to the second.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that the res/modus distinction alone sorts predicates and names a gap, and c010 as worded claims only that it provides 'the resources' to ground meaning. But your rejoinder runs two standards together, and I want to separate them. Exclusion narrows; it does not fill. I concede that. Still, Aquinas's own practice treats 'one' as having content through the via negativa and eminence together, not through a definition of divine oneness [W4206101892.a2]. Maren can preach that God is one in the sense that God is not divided into parts, not a composite of essence and existence, and not one among many, and that this unity is the source of all creaturely unity. Those are positive claims about the res, and the priest can say them. What he cannot do is give a complete account of the res, and no theist's account of divine simplicity offers one. The open question in c038 concerns exactly this completeness gap, and the argument's own c005 claims 'sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice', which I read as the second standard, not the first. I take that as a real weakness: the argument does not establish that a priest knows what to say in full, only that he has determinate, if partial, content. I hold that the weaker standard is the one that matters for meaning, since meaning does not require complete specification.

Revised premise: The Thomistic framework supplies, via negation and eminence, determinate positive content for divine predicates sufficient for meaningful preaching and practice, though not a complete specification of the res significata.

turn.content:
You are right that the bare distinction does not by itself tell Father Maren what divine oneness positively consists in—it marks a formal gap. But the argument never claims the distinction alone performs that task; it introduces the distinction as a further resource within the broader analogical framework [W7172336769.c009], and the text explicitly acknowledges that the Fregean distinction alone does not provide a theory of meaning [W7172336769.c038]. The determinate content comes from the doctrine of analogy as a whole, which supplies principled constraints on admissible predications [W7172336769.c025], and from the fixed referent for 'God' that allows an intelligible account of divinity [W4206101892.a2]. The res significata is therefore not an empty placeholder: knowing that God is not composite and is the source of unity gives Maren genuinely constrained, if semantically open, content. The distinction sorts the predicate into its proper analogical mode; the broader framework fills the divine slot. So the framework does populate the res significata, but only when the distinction is read as operating within that larger semantic-metaphysical structure.

Revised premise: The res/modus distinction is a necessary formal tool within the analogical framework, yet the determinate content of the res significata is supplied by the broader metaphysical context—particularly the fixed referent of 'God' and the principled constraints of analogy—rather than by the distinction itself.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content: You press a real worry: if Ruth can only gesture at 'primary' analogy, the framework risks circularity. But you treat analogy as a purely semantic device, whereas the argument presents it as a semantic thesis grounded in the metaphysical relation that creatures participate in perfections pre-contained in God [W7172336769.c055]. That metaphysics fixes the truth-conditions: intrinsic perfection predication states what God is in Godself, so Essay A is true because wisdom is God's simple essence, while Essay B falsely imposes a creaturely mode [W7172336769.c070]. Nadia's Fregean concern is addressed by locating sense in the modus significandi determined by this metaphysics: multiple attributes are different senses of the same simple referent [W7172336769.c036], and the relation stops regress [W7172336769.c057]. You are right that the semantic vocabulary alone does not specify content; the argument survives only because the semantic is inseparable from the metaphysical grounding [W7172336769.c009]. Semantic openness remains [W7172336769.c005], but the content is sufficiently determinate because it is metaphysically fixed, not lexically opaque.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content:
Your reply moves the determinacy from the lexicon into metaphysics, but it does not show that the metaphysics is available to Ruth as a criterion. Ruth's rubric must sort Essay A from Essay B. You say the truth-conditions are fixed because wisdom is God's simple essence and Essay B "falsely imposes a creaturely mode." Yet that verdict requires knowing which mode is God's and which is creaturely, and that is exactly what Tomas asked her to specify. Appealing to the metaphysical grounding relocates the question about the ratio of proportionality; it does not answer it.

Nor does the claim that multiple attributes are different senses of one simple referent help Nadia's question. If "wise" in Essay A and "wise" in Essay B both pick out the one simple essence, then the two essays do not differ in truth-value by reference, and you still owe a sense-level difference that Ruth can apply. Pointing to the modus significandi repeats the problem one level down.

So I grant that the metaphysics would fix content if it were independently determinate. The objection stands unless you can show that Ruth, without already knowing the answer, can apply it to distinguish A from B.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You press a genuine gap. The argument claims intrinsic perfection predication states what God is in Godself [W7172336769.c070], that analogy is grounded in participation [W7172336769.c055], and that this metaphysical relation fixes meaning [W7172336769.c057]. But you are right that ontological determination is not operational determination: Ruth can formally exclude creaturely modes, yet the positive sense of 'wise' in Essay A remains specified only by negation and metaphysical participation, not by a Fregean sense she can independently articulate. The argument conflates metaphysical truth-making with practical criterion-giving. I concede that the argument as stated does not survive your challenge. To save it, one must add that the res significata/modus significandi distinction yields a practically applicable formal rule—exclude creaturely modes—so that competent practitioners can judge predications correctly even when the positive divine modus exceeds complete lexical specification.

Revised premise: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy provides a practically applicable formal rule through the res significata and modus significandi distinction—specifically, the exclusion of creaturely modes of signification—that allows competent practitioners to discriminate correct from incorrect divine predications even when the positive ratio of proportionality remains semantically open.

objection.text: Consider Ruth, a preacher in a rural congregation, who tells her flock that God is 'good' and, when asked what this means, answers: 'God is not like the good things we see, which come mixed with defect; God's goodness is the source of all goodness, and far exceeds it.' Her hearers leave with a usable sense: do not treat God's goodness as a quality that could be lost, outweighed, or matched by a rival. Now a parishioner, Tom, asks whether God's goodness might be compatible with God permitting a child's suffering for reasons God alone knows. Ruth's framework offers only negation and eminence: God is not defective, and God's goodness exceeds our notion. It yields no verdict. Tom cannot decide whether to trust God in his grief, nor what a 'good' God would or would not do. The negations exclude defect but leave every positive question about divine action open. The worry about meaning arises precisely at the point where practice requires positive content, and eminence only restates that content is beyond reach.

objection.text: A parish council must decide whether to shelter refugees. They ask their pastor whether God commands hospitality. Under the Thomistic analogical framework, 'hospitable' is deemed admissible and said primarily of God, while 'cruel' is excluded. Yet the framework assigns no truth-conditional sense to 'God is hospitable': it does not specify whether divine hospitality welcomes all strangers unconditionally or only the righteous. Because the council cannot derive any actionable content from the predicate beyond its bare label, they remain unable to decide whether turning families away violates God's nature. The formal constraint on admissible words therefore fails to guide practice; without at least partial truth-conditional content, the distinction between primary and derivative predication collapses into a mere lexical permission list. The promised determinacy for practice is illusory.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that r2 concedes the absence of truth-conditional sense for each predicate, so the argument never promised that 'God is hospitable' settles whether to shelter families. Its claim is narrower: the framework fixes which predicates are said primarily of God and which derivatively, and that is enough for practice in the sense that a community can rule out predications that would contradict the admitted ones (for example, that God's hospitality is cruel), while leaving the finer question open. The pastor can say that turning away the destitute stranger is at odds with what is said primarily of God, even without a full specification of the res significata [W7172336769.c004][W7172336769.c025]. Still, your point lands on the conclusion: 'sufficiently determinate for practice' overstates what a constraint-only framework delivers. A permission list that excludes 'cruel' does guide action in cases where the act is plainly cruel, but it is silent on the borderline case you describe, and the author's own open question concedes that determinate truth-conditions are not yet supplied [W7172336769.c038]. So the argument survives only as a weaker claim: constraint for practice, not determinacy sufficient to decide hard cases. I concede that the conclusion as worded, and the 'practice' claim in r2, must be narrowed.

The disagreement does show something, though: the constraint excludes 'God is evil' and 'God is a chair' [W7172336769.c025], but it does not adjudicate between two admissible, eminent goodnesses. So the dispute is a live test of whether 'sufficient for practice' has teeth. I think it does, in one respect: both brothers are forced to reason from a shared picture of goodness as ordered toward the divine good, which is the sense in which the doctrine ties meaning to metaphysics rather than to free stipulation. Yet that is a constraint on the reasoning, not a verdict. I concede the argument as stated overreaches if c042 is read as claiming determinacy sufficient to resolve doctrinal disputes; the defensible claim is narrower, and the objection shows that narrower claim is all the framework can bear.

objection.text: Two Thomist theologians, both trained in the analogical framework with its res significata/modus significandi distinction, disagree about whether 'God suffers' is a legitimate predication. The first argues that suffering, as the patient's proper response to love's rejection, is said analogically of God: the res significata (loving endurance of evil) is properly divine, only the modus significandi (passive reception) is creaturely. He concludes that a pastoral worker should tell a grieving mother that God truly shares her pain. The second theologian, using the same framework, insists that suffering involves potency and composition, which are contrary to what is said primarily of God—simplicity and impassibility—so the predication must be excluded entirely, and the pastoral worker should instead say that God is present to her suffering without himself suffering. Both reason within the analogical framework; neither violates its stated constraints. The framework provides no principled mechanism for deciding which of these predications is 'contrary to what is said primarily of God,' because that determination itself depends on prior, non-analogically-settled judgments about which divine attributes are primary.

It does not claim that these constraints exclude ALL non-admissible predications or that they handle every metaphorical or symbolic use of language in sermons. The objection attacks a stronger, universal-exclusion version of the premise that the argument does not assert. Moreover, revised premise r3 explicitly states the framework 'does not by itself settle contested cases,' confirming the argument does not claim exhaustive coverage of all possible predications.
